## What's the story?

In 2023, Florida homeowners were paying [the most](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2023/jul/18/donald-trump/trump-is-correct-that-florida-has-highest-home-ins/) for home insurance in the country, in part due to the susceptibility of the state to hurricanes, but also, according to the insurance industry, because of an overly plaintiff-friendly litigation environment. Regardless, insurers in Florida were not doing well financially, a risk which they passed onto consumers by hiking rates. It wasn't enough. Six insurers [went insolvent](https://www.cbsnews.com/miami/news/sixth-florida-property-insurer-declared-insolvent/) in Florida in 2022, and the year after, Farmers Insurance [left the state altogether](https://www.cnn.com/2023/07/12/business/farmers-insurance-florida). In response, the state [passed](https://floir.gov/newsroom/archives/item-details/2023/05/31/icymi-governor-desantis-signs-consumer-protection-legislation-to-support-florida-policyholders-when-disaster-strikes) reforms in 2022 and 2023 that were intended to lower premiums for Floridians by changing claims handling processes. The Sun Sentinel and Orlando Sentinel are interested in analyzing **how homeowners' insurance coverage has changed for Floridians and whether they are paying more for less.**

As a first step, the newsrooms are interested in determining how policy cancellations and non-renewal rates have changed. A recent analysis of data from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) by Weiss Ratings, an insurance rating industry, [found](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/homeowners-in-florida-and-california-dropped-by-their-insurance-companies-at-highest-rate-in-nation-302597819.html) that Florida homeowners have the highest rate of policy cancellations in the country. Using public data from the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation (FLOIR), I will analyze proportions of policy cancellations and non-renewals for the top insurers in the state, normalized by the overall number of written policies.

##### 🏠 Why does this matter?

As the litigation environment has become less favorable for plaintiffs, homeowners have less recourse to fight cancellations or non-renewals. If more policies (or a similar number of policies) are being cancelled, more Floridians may be put in a situation where they have to pay more for a different insurer, opt for less coverage to save on premiums or may forgo insurance altogether if they have paid their mortgage. When the next big hurricane strikes, which is all but inevitable in Florida, there may be fewer homeowners who can recoup the damages to their homes.

This analysis will also hold the industry and Florida lawmakers to account by critically analyzing the claims by the insurance industry that the 2022-23 reforms resulted in lower premiums for Floridians. A recent report [found](https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/us/news/property/floridians-pay-181-more-for-home-insurance-than-us-average--report-571385.aspx) that Floridians still pay the most for home insurance in the country, and a report by the advocacy group Coalition for an Insurable Future [found](https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/environment/climate-change/article315840623.html) that premiums went up, even more than the national rate. To test the assumption that premiums are just as expensive or even more expensive than before the reforms, I will use estimated premium data from a [National Bureau of Economic Research paper](https://benkeys.github.io/insurance_data/). If it turns out that premiums have not meaningfully changed, it would be harder for the insurance industry and Florida lawmakers to justify the reforms that worsened consumer protections.

##### 🌀 Why now?

Hurricane season for Florida has just started, which [runs from June to November](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/refresh.shtml?epac). Extreme weather events are becoming more common around the world, and so Florida is becoming an increasingly costly environment to do business for insurers. As a result, Floridians are dominated by Florida-only insurers, a state insurance program or people going without insurance altogether. Others may leave the state altogether. Last December, a [survey](https://business.fau.edu/departments/economics/business-economics-polling/bepi-polls/bepi-polls-2025/florida-american-dream.php) by the Business and Economic Polling Initiative at Florida Atlantic University found that a quarter were "seriously" considering leaving the state, for a number of reasons. 

## Have insurance premiums gone down?

To determine whether premiums have indeed lowered as a result of the 2022-23 reforms, I used data from a [National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) paper](https://benkeys.github.io/insurance_data/) which estimated premiums for each county from mortgage escrow payments, which authors said they were able to extract insurance-related payments. They in turn obtained this escrow data from CoreLogic (now [Cotality](https://www.cotality.com/)), a property data and analytics provider.

The following is a snapshot of estimated premiums for 2024 across the state, showing higher estimated premiums for coastal counties in South Florida.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code"

library(leaflet)
pr24 <- read.csv("../data/nber-property-insurance-expenditures-2024-county.csv")
flor_prm_24 <- pr24 %>% dplyr::filter(StateAbb=="FL")

flor_prm_24 <- flor_prm_24 %>%
  mutate(FIPS = sprintf("%05d", FIPS))

dw_data <- flor_prm_24 %>%
  select(FIPS, NAME, median_premium)

#write.csv(dw_data, "../data/county_premiums_24.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```

### Read in the full NBER estimated premiums data
Extending the analysis to the full date range from 2014 to 2024, it is clear that premiums did not meaningfully *reduce* after 2022-23 legislative reforms. This may be in part because of major hurricanes in 2024 that could have cancelled out legislation-related savings. Data from 2025 is forthcoming, and I have reached out to the authors who told the previous intern a month ago that it would be uploaded soon.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code"

years <- 2014:2024

files <- sprintf("../data/nber-property-insurance-expenditures-%d-county.csv", 2014:2024)

premiums_allyears <- NULL

for (yr in 2014:2024) {
  filename <- paste0("../data/nber-property-insurance-expenditures-", yr, "-county.csv")
  df <- read.csv(filename)
  df$year <- yr
  premiums_allyears <- rbind(premiums_allyears, df)
}

fl_allyears <- premiums_allyears |>
  dplyr::filter(StateAbb == "FL") |>
  select(year, NAME, median_premium) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = NAME, values_from = median_premium)

#write.csv(fl_allyears, "../data/county_premiums_all.csv")

```

## Have cancellations and non-renewals increased?

The Florida Office of Insurance Regulation publishes quarterly [Residential Market Share Reports](https://floir.gov/tools-and-data/residential-market-share-reports) from Q2 2022 to Q4 2025, broken down by insurer and policy type. We are most interested in the variables that relate to **cancellations** and **non-renewals**.

::: callout-note
## Key terms (Source: FLOIR)

**Cancelled**: Policies in which either the policyholder or the insurer decides to stop coverage before the expiration date of the policy. All policies transferred to other corporations, including subsidiaries with a separate book of business, should be reported as canceled.

**Non-Renewed**: Occurs when the policy expires and either the policyholder or the insurer decides not to continue the same coverage. This does not include policies canceled.

**Hurricane Risk cancelled/non-renewed**: Policies that are canceled by the insurer for the purpose of reducing exposure to hurricane claims.
:::

Here's what the landscape looked like in the most recent report, the first quarter of 2026, after a little cleaning to drop irrelevant columns:

## Data Dictionary

| Column name                  | Definition                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **Policies in Force**        | Snapshot as of the last day of the reporting quarter. Total policies in force across all coverage types.                                                                                                                          |
| **Wind-Covered Policies**    | Snapshot as of the last day of the reporting quarter. Policies in force that include wind coverage.                                                                                                                               |
| **Policies Canceled**        | Quarterly count. Policies in which either the policyholder or the insurer stopped coverage before the expiration date. Per FLOIR, also includes policies transferred to affiliated corporations with a separate book of business. |
| **Canceled Bc Hurr. Risk**   | Quarterly count. Subset of canceled policies where the insurer initiated the cancellation specifically to reduce hurricane exposure. Insurer-initiated only.                                                                      |
| **Policies Nonrenewed**      | Quarterly count. Policies where the term expired and either the policyholder or the insurer chose not to continue coverage. Does not include canceled policies.                                                                   |
| **Nonrenewed Bc Hurr. Risk** | Quarterly count. Subset of nonrenewed policies where the insurer initiated the nonrenewal specifically to reduce hurricane exposure. Insurer-initiated only.                                                                      |
| **New Policies Written**     | Quarterly count. New policies written where: (1) the risk was not previously insured by this carrier, (2) coverage materially changed from prior coverage, or (3) coverage was extended to the same policyholder.                 |
:::

### Load the full dataset (2022-2025)

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code"

by_policy_post_22_files <- list.files(
  path = "../data/raw/market_share_reports/by_policy_post_22_quarterly",
  full.names = TRUE
)

# create a list object of dataframes
by_policy_post_22_raw <- by_policy_post_22_files |> 
  # set the name to ####-q#
  set_names(~ str_extract(.x, "\\d{4}-q\\d{1,2}")) |> 
  map(
    \(x) read_excel(x, skip = 3) 
  )

### <helper functions> ###
clean_df <- function(input_df) {
  input_df %>%
    clean_names() %>%                                   
    mutate(across(where(is.character), tolower))       
}

remove_date <- function(col_name) {
  case_when(
    # when the col contains _as_of delete everything after that (dates)
    str_detect(col_name, "_as_of") ~ str_remove(col_name, "(?<=_as_of).*"),
    # when the col contains _in_the_three, delete everything after that
    str_detect(col_name, "_in_the_three") ~ str_remove(col_name, "(?<=_in_the_three).*"),
    # if it doesn't contain either string, then default to original col name
.default = col_name
)
}

### </helper functions> ###

# every dataframe starts on row 3
by_policy_post_22_raw <- by_policy_post_22_raw |> 
  map(
    # apply clean_df() function to lower everything and clean up text
    \(x) clean_df(x)
  )

# making colnames consistent then binding dataframes into master quarterly
by_policy_post_22 <- by_policy_post_22_raw |> 
  # applying remove_date function across all dataframes on all cols to remove dates
  map(
    \(x) rename_with(x, remove_date) |> 
      # edited by JL
      mutate(across(
        -c(company_name, naic_code, policy_type),
        as.numeric
      ))
  ) |> 
  bind_rows(.id = "quarter")

homeowner_policies <- c(
  "personal residential - condominium unit owners",
  "personal residential - homeowners (excl tenant and condo) - owner occupied",
  "personal residential - tenants",
  "personal residential - mobile homeowners",
  "personal residential - farmowners",
  "personal residential - allied lines - wind only dwellings",
  "personal residential - condominium unit owners - wind only",
  "personal residential - homeowners (excl tenant and condo) - owner occupied - wind only",
  "personal residential - mobile homeowners - wind only",
  "personal residential - tenants - wind only",
  "personal residential - allied lines"
)

homeowner_policies_post_22 <- by_policy_post_22 |> 
  dplyr::filter(policy_type %in% homeowner_policies) |> #filter by homeowner
  # sum across all homeowner-related policies
  group_by(quarter, naic_code, company_name) |> 
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ sum(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop")

# clean up colnames and drop unneeded cols
hp <- homeowner_policies_post_22 |>
  rename(
    policies_snapshot     = total_number_of_policies_in_force_as_of,
    canceled_cumulative   = total_number_of_policies_canceled_in_the_three,
    nonrenewed_cumulative = total_number_of_policies_nonrenewed_in_the_three,
    new_cumulative        = total_number_of_new_policies_written_in_the_three,
    received_cumulative   = total_number_of_policies_received_from_other_insurers_in_the_three,
    transferred_cumulative = total_number_of_policies_transferred_to_other_insurers_in_the_three
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year        = as.integer(str_sub(quarter, 1, 4)),
    quarter_num = as.integer(str_extract(quarter, "(?<=q)\\d+"))
  ) |>
  select(
    quarter, year, quarter_num,
    naic_code, company_name,
    policies_snapshot,
    canceled_cumulative, nonrenewed_cumulative,
    new_cumulative, received_cumulative,
    transferred_cumulative
  )

```

Then combine quarters to get annual data:

```{r}
insurer_annual <- hp |>
  arrange(naic_code, year, quarter_num) |>
  group_by(naic_code, year) |>
  summarise(
    across(ends_with("_cumulative"), ~ sum(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    policies_snapshot = dplyr::last(policies_snapshot),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

```

The main calculations of interest:

$$\scriptsize
\text{Proportion canceled} = \frac{\text{Policies canceled that year}}{\text{Policies in force at start of year} + \text{New policies written} + \text{Policies received from other insurers}}
$$

$$\scriptsize
\text{Proportion nonrenewed} = \frac{\text{Policies nonrenewed that year}}{\text{Policies in force at start of year} + \text{New policies written} + \text{Policies received from other insurers}}
$$

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code"
industry_annual <- insurer_annual |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    across(ends_with("_cumulative"), ~ sum(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    policies_snapshot = sum(policies_snapshot, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(
    annual_policies = dplyr::lag(policies_snapshot, 1) + new_cumulative + received_cumulative,
    prop_canceled   = if_else(annual_policies == 0, NA_real_, canceled_cumulative   / annual_policies),
    prop_nonrenewed = if_else(annual_policies == 0, NA_real_, nonrenewed_cumulative / annual_policies)
  )

insurer_annual <- insurer_annual |>
  group_by(naic_code) |>
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    annual_policies = dplyr::lag(policies_snapshot, 1) + new_cumulative + received_cumulative,
    prop_canceled   = if_else(annual_policies == 0, NA_real_, canceled_cumulative   / annual_policies),
    prop_nonrenewed = if_else(annual_policies == 0, NA_real_, nonrenewed_cumulative / annual_policies)
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

### Debugging sanity check

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code"
# For every year, industry_annual$policies_snapshot should equal
# the sum of all insurers' snapshots in insurer_annual
snapshot_check <- insurer_annual |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(insurer_sum = sum(policies_snapshot, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(industry_annual |> select(year, policies_snapshot), by = "year") |>
  mutate(match = near(insurer_sum, policies_snapshot))

stopifnot("Bug 1: industry snapshot != sum of insurer snapshots" = all(snapshot_check$match, na.rm = TRUE))

# For every insurer-year, annual_policies should equal
# THAT insurer's prior-year snapshot + current-year new + received.
# Self-join insurer_annual to itself with a 1-year offset to get the expected lag.
lag_check <- insurer_annual |>
  select(naic_code, year, policies_snapshot) |>
  mutate(year_next = year + 1) |>
  rename(prior_snapshot = policies_snapshot) |>
  right_join(
    insurer_annual |> select(naic_code, year, annual_policies, new_cumulative, received_cumulative),
    by = join_by(naic_code, year_next == year)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    expected_annual_policies = prior_snapshot + new_cumulative + received_cumulative,
    match = near(annual_policies, expected_annual_policies) | 
      (is.na(annual_policies) & is.na(expected_annual_policies))
  )

stopifnot("Bug 2: lag walked across insurers, not across years" = all(lag_check$match, na.rm = TRUE))

```

### Data cleaning

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code"

names_lookup <- hp |>
  group_by(naic_code) |>
  arrange(year, quarter_num, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(naic_code, company_name)

insurer_annual <- insurer_annual |>
  left_join(names_lookup, by = "naic_code")

```

## Potential considerations

Potential considerations when attempting to adequately addressing the hypothesis:

-   Premium data from the NBER paper is only estimated rather than directly reported by consumers or insurers. The newsrooms plan to run a survey to collect homeowners' experiences. While this will be anecdotal, it will still be helpful to complement these analyses.

-   Hurricanes Helene and Milton in fall 2024 were costly and likely cancelled out any reforms-driven changes in premiums. Data for 2025 premiums from the NBER authors does not exist yet, but I have reached out to the authors to ask for it (they told the previous intern a month ago that it would be uploaded soon).

-   *Either* the policyholder *or* the insurer can cancel and non-renew policies, making it difficult to attribute these actions specifically to industry decisions.

-   It looks like there is a data issue with at least one insurer, Clear Blue Insurance Company, which may be a data entry error on their end, which resulted in there being 130% policies calculated as non-renewed. However as this insurer had only a couple hundred policies, it would have been excluded anyway due to the analysis being limited to insurers which have 500 or more policies.

## Future work

The analysis of cancellations and non-renewals thus far is limited to the 2022-2025 period because that is the period covered by the "market share reports" data. A different data source exists for pre-2022 data called [Market Intelligence Reports](https://qsrng.floir.gov/reports/ReportViewer.aspx). This data source is much more incomplete as not all insurance carriers had data for every year, due to carriers invoking trade secret exemptions, which are detailed on [the FLOIR website.](https://floir.gov/tools-and-data/residential-market-share-reports) Future work will build on code written by the previous intern in order to extend the policy cancellation/non-renewal analyses further back in time.
